headline: A Republican forced a vote to impeach Hegseth.
summary: Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his seat, read eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor Monday. The main charge: fighting in Iran for more than 90 days without Congress's say-so. The House must vote within two legislative days. Hegseth: 'We're not worried about that.'

cover_question.q: Why go after one of their own?

cover_answer: One Republican. He says the Iran war broke the law.
table_question: Would you pick a fight you expect to lose, if you think it's right?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A man in Congress named Thomas Massie wants Pete Hegseth, who runs the military, to lose his job. He says Hegseth kept a war going that Congress never said yes to. This week Congress votes, like a class voting on who stays line leader. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: One man wants another's job gone, and a vote decides: the whole story at seven. The class vote is one they have sat through, so 'impeach' needs no defining.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script hands over one man who wants another to lose his job, and a class vote on line leader, which they have sat through. 'Impeach' never needs defining. Expect 'is he going to jail?' No. Losing a job and going to jail are different, and the vote has not happened yet.

8-12.script: Congress has to say yes before a war runs past 90 days. Massie says the Iran war passed that mark with no yes, so Hegseth broke the rule and should go. Impeachment is the referee's whistle: the House votes on the charge, then the Senate holds a trial. Only two cabinet members have ever been impeached.
8-12.why: Rule, breach, whistle, trial: a chain they can follow and argue about at ten.
8-12.why_long: At ten they work out rules and whether adults apply them, so the script hands over the rule (90 days, then Congress says yes), the breach Massie claims, a whistle in two stages. The Senate letting both past members off is what they seize on. Expect 'so what's the point?' Massie: he may lack the votes, and he's doing it anyway.

13-17.script: Massie says he may not have the votes and is doing it anyway, because it is right. Principle, or theater? He calls it a gentler version of what Democrats will do in January, and wants Trump to swap Hegseth out first. Second: if the Senate won't convict, did anything happen?
13-17.why: A vote that may fail and a warning that may work: both true. At fifteen they can hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the vote will likely fail, and Massie says the aim is to make Trump replace Hegseth before January, so a loss is fine. The script sets principle against theater. Expect 'why does Trump call him a loser?' Massie lost his seat and fought Trump on Iran. Neither settles it.

5-7.a: No. Impeachment is about losing a job, not jail. And the vote hasn't happened yet.

8-12.a: The House votes to charge an official. The Senate then tries the case.

8-12.q: Why does it matter if Congress said yes?
8-12.a: Congress declares war. Massie says 90 days in Iran with no yes breaks that law.

13-17.q: Why go after one of their own?
13-17.a: One Republican who lost his seat. He says the Iran war broke the law.
Massie doesn't know. The House is 218 to 214. Removal needs two-thirds of the Senate.
